By 23, he was generating $50M in sales.

That piece became Fanatics [@fanatics].

Today, Fanatics is tracking toward $13B in revenue, while Rubin’s annual Hamptons White Party attracts names like Tom Brady, Beyoncé, Jay-Z, Kim Kardashian and Drake.

From nearly bankrupt at 16 to hosting one of America’s most exclusive parties.

Meta paid $14.3 billion for half a company that started in a fridge.

Alexandr Wang was at MIT, and someone kept taking his yogurt. So he built a camera to catch them. The camera saw everything. It just couldn’t tell him who.

The AI had never been taught properly. Almost none of it had.

He dropped out at 19 and started Scale AI with Lucy Guo. Within a few years it was feeding data to self-driving cars, to OpenAI, and to the Pentagon. By 24 he was a billionaire.

Scale reached $870 million in revenue. Then Meta took 49% at a $29 billion valuation.

All from a missing yogurt.

segments.text: Mark Zuckerberg paid $14.3 billion to hire him, but it all started with a stolen yogurt.
Alexander Wang grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, surrounded by physicists, including both of his parents.
At 17, he made the U.S. physics team, then onto MIT.
But during his first year, his roommates kept stealing his yogurt.
So to fight back, Wang put a camera inside his fridge to catch the thief.
It failed, not because the code was broken, but because the AI had never been taught what yogurt actually looked like.
And that gave him an idea.
AI didn't just need better algorithms.
It needed better labeled data to learn from and understand exactly what it was looking at.
So at 19, Wang dropped out of MIT and co-founded Scale AI.
Soon, self-driving car companies were customers, then the U.S. Army, then Open AI.
By 24, Wang was the world's youngest self-made billionaire.
And in 2025, Meta invested $14.3 billion into Scale AI and brought Wang in to lead
its superintelligence efforts, all because someone kept stealing his yogurt.
Thank you.

Nike passed on Travis Grillo. That rejection helped create a $28M pickle empire.

In 2008, Grillo survived four Nike interviews and even sat down with Phil Knight.

No job came.

Back home in Connecticut, he tasted his grandfather Sam’s century-old pickle recipe and spotted a business nobody else saw.

Seven ingredients. Zero preservatives. One 1985 Oldsmobile.

He packed the trunk and sold jars by hand at parks, courts and ballfields.

Boston officials said he wouldn’t last an hour.

Then Whole Foods called.

By 2019, @grillospickles had reached 10,000+ stores and roughly $28 million in annual sales.

Sometimes the door that closes is the one that forces you to build your own.

In 2008, he had four interviews with Nike to become a sneaker designer.
Even met co-founder Phil Knight.
They still said no.
He went home to Norwich, Connecticut, sat in his parents' backyard, and ate his grandfather,
Sam's homemade pickles, a recipe over 100 years old, seven ingredients, and no preservatives.
That's when the idea hit him.
Why not sell these?
He loaded up his 1985 Oldsmobile and started driving to baseball fields and basketball courts
across Connecticut, selling pickles straight from the trunk.
Most people thought he was crazy.
His friends told him to try Boston.
The health department said he wouldn't last an hour.
He built a pickle cart anyway and started selling on Boston Common, two spears for a dollar.
Many of his first customers were people experiencing homelessness in the park.
Then Whole Foods noticed.
They ordered, he delivered it himself, and it sold out.
Buyout offers followed.
He rejected everyone that wanted him to add preservatives.
By 2019, Grillo's was in 10,000 stores doing $28 million a year.
In 2021, King's Hawaiian acquired it.
Today, it's America's number one refrigerated pickle brand.
It all started with a no.

At 24, Abdul Samad Rabiu came home to save a collapsing family business. Four decades later, his fortune briefly approached $20 billion.

His father had been detained. Operations were falling apart. Suppliers were losing confidence.

Rabiu rebuilt trust, stabilized the company, then launched BUA International in 1988.

First came steel. Then sugar. Then cement.

BUA developed one of sub-Saharan Africa’s largest sugar refineries and invested $900 million into cement production.

Even when currency losses erased his billionaire status, he kept building quietly.

By 2025, BUA Foods’ profit had surged 95%. BUA Cement’s jumped 382%.

He returned home to protect a family legacy, and turned it into one of Africa’s most powerful business empires.

Vicky Tsai built Tatcha from the kind of place most people never come back from.

Before the skincare brand sold to Unilever for a reported $500 million in 2019, she had a Harvard MBA, a Wall Street career, and skin so damaged by stress that she was using steroids every day.

Nothing helped.

So she left her job and went to Kyoto, where a geisha introduced her to Japanese beauty rituals that had been passed down for generations.

Back in the U.S., retailers told her Asian beauty was too niche.

So Vicky sold her engagement ring, car, and furniture, moved into her parents’ house, and started Tatcha [@tatcha] from a garage.

Nine years without a salary.

$600,000 in debt.

Still, she kept going.

Meet Vicki Tsai.
She had a Harvard MBA and a career as a derivatives trader on Wall Street.

She couldn't believe this didn't exist back home.
When she pitched retailers, they told her Asian beauty wasn't aspirational in the US.
Too niche, too exotic, nobody wanted it.
So she sold her engagement ring, her car, and her furniture,

Tacha launched from the garage the same day her daughter was born.
For the next nine years, Vicki didn't take a single salary and at one point was over $600,000 in debt, but the products worked.
Tacha landed in Sephora and by 2015 was the 21st fastest growing private company in America.
In 2019, Unilever acquired it for a reported $500 million.

In May 2024, the chain filed for bankruptcy. 93 locations were gone, and the brand looked like another American restaurant giant fading out.

Three months later, Damola Adamolekun @damolaadamolekun stepped in.

Born in Nigeria and raised across three continents, he had already run P.F. Chang’s at 31, helping pull it back to $1 billion in revenue during COVID.

Before taking the job, he quietly visited Red Lobster locations himself.

He found tired dining rooms, stretched staff, and a company people had started writing off.

One year later, sales are up 40%.

Now he says this could become the greatest comeback in restaurant history.

In 1971, her family fled Indonesia and landed near Buffalo with nothing.

Her dad, a dentist back home, started washing dishes.
Her mom, a nurse, picked up waitress shifts.

From zero, they rebuilt. Theresia turned that pressure into fuel.

First in her high school to get into Brown.
MBA at Stanford.
Then Silicon Valley.

In 2005, she’s in the room when her firm places an early bet on a tiny college network called Facebook.

That bet made history.

She went on to launch Acrew Capital, now a major force in early-stage venture.

Forbes named her: first female billionaire in venture capital.

Her parents handed her a shot.

She turned it into history.

Nobody saw it coming.
Least of all the industry she'd go on to change.
Teresa Gao was three years old when her family fled Indonesia in 1971 and landed in a small town near Buffalo with almost nothing.
Her father had been a dentist back home.
In America, he washed dishes.
Her mother waitress.
They rebuilt from zero and made sure their daughter saw exactly what that took.
She got into Brown, graduated at the top of her class, then an MBA from Stanford,
and eventually landed at one of Silicon Valley's most powerful investment firms where she became their first female partner.
Then, in 2005, a 21-year-old Mark Zuckerberg walked in with a pitch, a college social network, barely 10 people on the team.
Teresa was in the room when her firm wrote the check.
Forbes later estimated she held around 8 million Facebook shares at its IPO in 2012.
Most, a win like that would be enough. Not for Teresa. In 2014, she walked away to build her own firm and in 2019 launched Agru Capital, which now manages $1.7 billion in investments.
83% of its founding team are women or people of color. In 2025, Forbes made it official.
Teresa Gao, $1.2 billion net worth. Not just America's first female billionaire investor, the first in the history of the industry.

His grandpa paid $4,700 for a hearing aid that barely worked.

So Ramin Syed and two McMaster classmates built one for $20.

The idea started after Ramin watched his grandfather struggle to hear for 18 months. When the device finally arrived, it was noisy, expensive, and disappointing.

So they studied the ear itself.

Instead of building another tiny computer, they designed @amanolabs to work with the ear’s natural ability to amplify sound.

It’s 3D-printed, custom-made from an ear photo and a quick hearing test.

Cost to make: $1.

Retail price: $20.

Now they’re testing with Harvard Medical School.

Three students saw a broken industry and made it harder to defend.

description:
He turned a bus driver’s wage into a £4.5 billion business empire.

Anwar Pervez arrived in England from Pakistan in 1956, aged 21, and found work driving buses.

By 1963, he had saved enough to open a small shop in west London, selling spices and halal meat.

But the real shift came when he noticed who kept walking through the door: other shopkeepers.

So he stopped thinking only like a retailer.

In 1976, he opened Bestway Wholesale in Acton, supplying small stores with cheaper stock at scale.

That single warehouse grew into a group spanning wholesale, cement, pharmacies, convenience stores and banking.

By 2022, Bestway had 8,750 employees and 12 million customers.

From one shop counter to Sir Anwar.

And it started on a bus in Bradford.
Meet Anwar Purvez.
In 1956, at 21 years old, he left Pakistan with almost nothing and took a job driving buses in England.
It was progress.
But Anwar wanted more than a driver's seat.
In 1963, he opened a small shop in West London selling Masala and Halalbi.
But noticed the high street had most of the customers, not him.
So he didn't go deeper into one shot.
He opened 10.
Then he stopped thinking like a shopkeeper, but someone who supplies them.
In 1976, he opened Best Way Wholesale and Acton.
One warehouse selling stock cheaper and serving small shopkeepers better than anyone else.
It paid off.
Warehouses spread across Britain through the 80s and 90s.
Then came pharmacies, cement, banking, and convenience stores.
By 2022, the group hit 4.5 billion pounds with 28,000 employees, and 10,000.
12 million customers across the UK, Pakistan, and the Middle East.
The former bus driver is now Sir Anwar Pervez, knighted in 1999.
In 2025, King Charles hosted him at Royal Ascot as he turned 90.
From bus shifts in Bradford to 4.5 billion pounds, one corner shop at a time.

description:
In 1999, the very first Coachella lost roughly $850,000, and founder Paul Tollett sold his house and car just to keep going.

Tollett came up in Pomona, a college student who got obsessed with live music promotion. Before he finished his degree, he dropped out to work concerts full time.

He later took over @goldenvoice, where he faced bigger rivals with deeper budgets and stronger artist ties.

So rather than compete on their terms, he built something of his own.

A festival where the lineup and the experience were the whole draw.

He drew inspiration from European festivals like Glastonbury, then carried that model to the California desert.

Plenty of people doubted it.

Today, Coachella ranks among the most successful music festivals on the planet, pulling in hundreds of millions a year and standing as a global cultural institution.

Some ideas only look crazy until enough time passes to make them look obvious.

By the mid-90s, they struggled as bigger festivals crushed them, so in 1997,
Talit flew to Glastonbury Festival and handed out pamphlets, showing sunny California to every manager he could find.
They laughed at the idea, but Talit believed in something nobody else at the time did,
that the festival itself could become the attraction.
Then Woodstock 99 happened, violence, arson, chaos.
Insurance costs jumped 40% just when Talit announced Coachella.
Beck, Rage Against the Machine and Tool, headlined to 25,000 people.
The crowd loved it.
But Golden Voice lost $850,000.
To keep the company alive, Talit sold his house, then his car, and later said it also cost him his marriage.
He came back in his marriage.
By 2017, Coachella became the first festival in history to gross over $100 million in a single year.
This year, $200 million across 250,000 attendees.
Tickets that once cost $50 dollars now start at $549.
Not bad for a college dropout whose vision was laughed at.

Meet Beckett to Haiti and Derek Webster.
Beckett first dreamed of helping people find affordable apartments in fifth grade.
After following his father through exhausting apartment searches across Brooklyn,

And after seeing it firsthand, one question kept bothering him.
How could anyone be expected to live in these conditions, let alone afford them?
Something had to change.
So years later, Beckett taught himself how to code using YouTube tutorials,
and AI tools, while his classmate Derek Webster Jr.
built the email system that would power the platform.
Together, they launched the tool Beckett's own family had once desperately needed.
A simple website that scrapes real estate listings to help users find below-market apartments
and rent-stabilized homes.
They quietly launched it on Reddit.

as people shared the link, tagged friends, and even thanked them for helping them finally find a
place to live. Soon after, their first subscribers covered their running costs, a local agent
paid them $1,000 to advertise on the platform, and Startup Accelerator Autos stepped in with
up to $25,000 to back their mission.
But even after tasting early success, the two founders are keeping their feet firmly
on the ground, balancing school during the day and building their startup late into the night.

Meet Dravya Shah.
While most kids his age were studying for exams,
Dravia spent his time on Twitter experimenting with code and building tools for fun.
And it was there that he built a simple bot that could transform tweets into images,
a small project that unexpectedly exploded online.
Soon after launching it, the bot went viral.
And Dravia did what most young builders dream about.
He sold it, pocketed the profit, and booked a one-way ticket from India to the United States to study at Arizona State.
But instead of slowing down, once he got there, he made a promise to himself.
Build something new every week and keep going for 40 weeks straight.
Week after week, he kept shipping.
Then on week 37, he built a tool that let people chat with their Twitter bookmarks.
And that small experiment would eventually grow into something much bigger.
That project became super memory, a tool designed to help AI recall and remember past conversations.
essentially building the memory layer for AI systems.
It didn't take long for the idea to catch the attention of some of the biggest names in tech,
including Google AI Chief Jeff Dean and Cloudflare's CTO,
ultimately leading to a $3 million seed round.
Not bad for a 20-year-old who started by building Twitter bots in his bedroom.

Eddy started Build with a simple mission.

Train robots to do human-like work.

How?

Xu asks factory workers to wear smart glasses, their shifts get recorded, and the steps get taught to
robots.

Build has so far generated over 2,500 clips and ~400,000 steps to train robots on everyday tasks.

The promise is fewer boring chores for people and steadier output for factories.

The risk is harder to ignore.

Because in his eyes, building the robots was never the hardest part.
Teaching them how to work was.
So he built a system that strapped smart glasses onto factory workers, capturing exactly how they do their jobs.
Every movement, every step, every decision, turning all of it into training data.
That data is then used to train robots.
to do the same work as the factory workers.

Now, Eddie's company has collected more than 2,500 clips and 400,000 human actions from workers across Asia,
and is preparing to expand into the US.
But as the age of robotics accelerates, one question remains, if robots can do everything humans can, where does that leave humans?

In 1967, a 16-year-old called Shahid Khan landed in Illinois during a blizzard with $500 in his pocket. His first job was washing dishes for $1.20 an hour.

While studying engineering, he got hired at a small auto parts company. He noticed their truck bumpers could be better, so he designed a one-piece bumper that was lighter, stronger, and cheaper to make.

He left, started his own company, then bought his former employer two years later.

By the late 1980s, his company was the sole bumper supplier for every Toyota sold in America. Today it turns over $9 billion a year.

Then he bought the Jacksonville Jaguars for $770 million, becoming the first ethnic-minority owner in NFL history, before going on to own premier league club Fulham, and All Elite Wrestling.

Forbes said it best, describing Khan’s journey as as the embodiment of the American Dream.

segments.text: This Pakistani immigrant went from washing dishes to building a $10 billion plus empire.
Meet Shahid Khan.
At 16, he arrived in America with just $500 and took a $1.20 an hour dishwashing job to survive.
But while studying engineering, he started working at a small auto parts company called Flex Engate.
That's where he noticed a simple problem others ignored.
Parts could be made better and cheaper.
So in 1978, he took a risk, borrowed $50,000, added his own savings, and started his own company.
His first big break came when General Motors became his customer.
Then, he made the move that changed everything.
